nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Richmond, Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world, and the Southern and Mid-Atlantic review and magazine culture of the 1830s and 1840s
literary_identity: Poet, tale-writer, reviewer and editor; the most exacting and most combative American critic of his generation, the maker of the analytical and the tales of horror, and the poet of the pure musical lyric, who attempted to live wholly by the pen in a country that had not yet a paying market for it.
biography: Poe was born Edgar Poe at Boston, the second of three children of travelling actors, and was left fatherless and motherless in early childhood: David Poe deserted the family, and his mother Elizabeth, an actress of Richmond, died there in 1811, after which he was taken into the household of John Allan, a wealthy Richmond tobacco merchant, from whom he took his middle name but who never adopted him. He went with the Allan family to England in 1815, was schooled in London and its neighbourhood, and returned to Richmond a boy formed on the Byron models and on the German tale then reaching America in translation. At the University of Virginia, which he entered in 1826 on Allan's terms, he contracted gambling debts that Allan refused to discharge; he broke with his foster father, removed to Boston, where his first slim volume of verse appeared without his name in 1827, served a short time in the United States army under an assumed name, and obtained through Allan's interest an appointment to the Military Academy at West Point, which he was deliberately dismissed from in the spring of 1831. Comes of age and without a fortune, he resolved to live by his pen, and the early 1830s found him contributing poems, tales and reviews to the annuals and magazines of the Southern and Middle States, with the collected volume of 1831, printed by subscription and prefaced by an attack upon the current American poets, as his profession of faith. He became editor of the Southern Literary Messenger at Richmond in 1835, and by his tales, his poems and his reviews made it the most widely circulated American monthly of its day; there followed the New York and Philadelphia years, employment on the magazines of those cities, and in 1840 the two-volume collection of his tales, which established the prose reputation that then carried him far beyond his verse. In 1836 he had married at Richmond his cousin Virginia Clemm, a child of thirteen, whose mother kept house with them; her long consumption and her death in 1847 left him, in his own account, without any tie. He edited a short-lived journal at New York in 1845, lectured on poetry and on the material universe, printed his prosimetrical cosmology in 1848, and projected a magazine of his own that was never funded. He was found in a state of insensibility at Baltimore in the first days of October 1849, on his way to remove to the city where his father's family lived, and died there on 7 October, aged forty; the circumstances of those last days have never been settled, and the friend who printed his works at length after him did so with a malicious preface which governed his reputation for a generation.
literary_profile: Within the range of this installment his work is the verse of three pamphlets and volumes - the first anonymous booklet, the longer poem of the star-island and the collected volume of 1831 with its short lyrics of classical beauty and its vision of the doomed city; afterwards came the tales, the poems of the later magazines, the criticism, the essay on the principle of composition and the prose of the cosmic argument. He wrote the analytical tale of ratiocination and the tale of nervous horror, the hoaxes and the marginal criticism of his own review work, and he projected, in his criticism of contemporary American books, the first serious American account of the poetical principle. His career as an editor is part of his work: the monthly, the annual, the magazine and the projected review are the forms in which he wrote.
stylistic_characteristics: In verse an intense and deliberate music, with internal rhyme, refrain, repetition of key words and an incantatory regularity of stanza, a command of the short lyric of address and of the long meditative or narrative poem; in prose an analytical first person, a nervous precision of detail, an art of suspense and anticlimax, and a criticism of bludgeon irony - abrupt, technical, and personal in attack, with a habit of defining his own practice against that of the traffic in magazines.
intellectual_concerns: Beauty as the sole province of the poem, and its exaltation into the supernal; the death of a beautiful woman as the most poetical of topics; the unity of effect and the economy of means by which a work of art should be constructed; the reach and the limits of analysis and of the calculating intellect; the isolation of the imaginative individual in a commercial letterscape; the material unity of the universe and the theological consequences of drawing it together.
historical_significance: He invented the analytical or detective tale and practised before anyone in English the short tale of single psychological effect; his theory of the poem, of the unity of impression and of the music of verse, passed by his French interpreters into the symbolist movement and so into the modern poetry of Europe, and his criticism created the model of the professional American reviewer. His tales of horror and of analysis founded durable native genres, and his career, cut short by a struggle with the economics of American periodical writing, became the standard case of the unhoused artist in a commercial republic.
major_influences: Lord Byron and the Byronic narrative poem
Charles Brockden Brown and the early American tale of the terrible
Matthew Gregory Lewis and the romance of terror
Samuel Taylor Coleridge's prose of the imagination and his criticism
Edward Young and the graveyard meditation
the German romantic tale and its American reviewers
the Richmond and Baltimore society and the periodical and annual market he wrote for
biographical_uncertainty: The identity of the woman addressed in the lyrics of beauty, and the chronology of his engagement to Sarah Helen Whitman, are variously stated; the quarrel and money history with John Allan is known largely from the Allans' side and from Poe's own complaints; the causes of the insensibility in which he was found at Baltimore, and the company he kept in the two or three days before his death, remain unexplained, and the evidence is disputed between intemperance, bodily disorder and the political violence of the election week. The printed obituary and the first collected edition were prepared by a literary enemy, and many anecdotes of the early life rest on his own jesting and on later reminiscence.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American, born in Scotland; the letters of revolutionary Philadelphia and of the western Pennsylvania frontier, the first American writer of that interior
literary_identity: Novelist, poet, playwright, orator, lawyer, judge, schoolmaster and founder of colleges; the inventor of the American picaresque comic novel of politics and settlement, and the most considerable man of letters of the Pennsylvania west before the 1830s.
biography: Brackenridge was born on the Kintyre peninsula near Campbeltown in Argyllshire, in the year 1748, of a Scottish family in straitened circumstances, and was carried by his parents to York County in Pennsylvania in the fifth year of his life. He grew up on the edge of the settlement, largely self-taught, herding cattle and picking up such learning as the country afforded until a neighbour recognized his capacity and helped him to books; he entered the college at Princeton, graduated in 1770, and gave himself afterwards to teaching, keeping a classical school and preparing young men for the college. He served the Revolutionary army as a chaplain, and about the same time began to publish verse, including a poem on the death of the general before Quebec which was recited and reprinted through the war years and gave him his first name in America. After the peace he removed to Philadelphia, read and practised law, wrote for the stage and the press, and about 1779 fixed himself in the western country, at first near Hannastown and afterwards about Pittsburgh, where the frontier supplied the society he satirized. There he founded an academy in 1787, the institution which became the university of the city, gave aid to the first newspaper of the west, and practised his profession before the county courts; he sat in the convention which framed the state constitution of the 1790s, and was made a judge of the courts of the western district. In the excise trouble of 1794 he rode with the militia, and tried at once to suppress the insurrection and to restrain the measures which had provoked it, and was reviled by the partisans of both sides; the controversy cost him his political standing and much of his professional business. His comic romance of Captain Farrago and his ragged Irish servant was put out in parts beginning in 1792, continued at intervals, and reissued in a revised and completed form shortly before his death; he wrote also a tragedy on the point of honour, sermons, orations and a quantity of controversial pamphlet matter, and he projected histories and plans of western education which he did not finish. His last years were clouded by the death of an elder son through intemperance, by his own increasing dependence on drink, by removed poverty and by quarrels with the neighbours among whom he had made his fortune, and he died on 25 June 1816 at Carlisle, whither he was journeying, and was buried there in the churchyard.
literary_profile: His central work is the long comic romance, begun in numbers and completed after more than twenty years, which follows a captain of militia and his servant through the elections, militias, speculations, sects and law circuits of the western republic, and which is the first American fiction to make popular politics and office-seeking its sustained subject. He wrote verse of the college and war occasion, including the funeral poem on the general at Quebec, a tragedy of honour and the duel, sermons and orations on education and on the diffusion of knowledge, and pamphlets on the insurrection and on the affairs of the west. Education was his lifelong scheme: the academy, the college, the school and the public library were for him the instruments by which a frontier country might be made a community, and his fiction is continuously an argument about learning, pretension and the uses of books.
stylistic_characteristics: A robust and colloquially various prose, moving between the high-flown rhetoric of the speculators and politicians, the blunt sense of the servant and the ironied narration of the author, with proverbs, misquotations, Latin school phrases and the speech of the courts and the back settlements all set against one another; an episodic and unhurried picaresque structure, tolerant of digressions and of essays within the story; and in the verse and the orations a fluent eighteenth-century diction of couplet and periodic sentence.
intellectual_concerns: The dangers and the promise of a republic without ranks, which has only invented new ones; office-seeking, demagogy and the pretensions of the wilder democracy; education and learning as the only safe foundation of western settlement; sectarian zeal and enthusiasm measured against reason and decency; the law, the militia and the conduct of the frontier; the claims of chivalry, honour and duelling in a country of common men.
historical_significance: He is the founder of the literature of the American interior and the author of the first American comic novel of politics, a book which carries the eighteenth-century picaresque across the mountains and applies it to the elections, speculations and sects of the new settlements. His academy became a university and his fiction is the beginning of a native tradition of the frontier satirists; the modern recovery of his work has placed him at the head of the line which runs to the comic storytellers of the Mississippi, and his career documents the intellectual history of the American west in the generation after the Revolution.
major_influences: Cervantes and the romance of adventure
Fielding and Smollett and the eighteenth-century comic epic in prose
the Augustan satire of Alexander Pope
the Scottish moral philosophy and divinity taught at Princeton
the frontier life of York County and the Pittsburgh country
the politics and law circuits of western Pennsylvania
the theatre and periodical press of Philadelphia in the 1780s
biographical_uncertainty: The year and place of his Scottish birth are given in the earliest memorials with small variations, the interval and conditions of his emigration rest on family narrative, and the chronology of the several parts and revised issues of his comic romance, and of the authorship of some pamphlets printed in his name, is still imperfectly settled.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Unitarian Boston review circle about the North American Review and the Harvard divinity and professoriate, and the New England editorial school of national records
literary_identity: Editor, biographer, historian, Unitarian minister and educator; the first American who made the documentary edition of the founding records a great national work, and the chief editor, teacher and institutional man of letters of the generation between the centennial and the Civil War.
biography: Sparks was born at Willington in the upland of Tolland County in Connecticut, the first of a large family of small means, and was put to school and to such Latin as the country afforded before his parents removed to the Ohio country while he was still a boy. There he taught, learned a little medicine and practised it, and read with that extraordinary diligence which made him a scholar without a college; after some years he returned east, was fitted for the college at the academy in New Hampshire, entered Harvard, and after his graduation studied for the ministry, being ordained a Unitarian minister and serving congregations in Massachusetts and in the west. From the first he combined preaching with authorship and editing: he wrote articles of history and biography for the journals, became connected with the North American Review at Boston and for some years conducted it, and at the same time planned the great work which gave him his fame - a collection of the letters and papers of the American ministers abroad during the Revolution, printed from the state records and furnished with notes and biographical and historical dissertations, in twelve volumes beginning in 1829. This was the first considerable documentary edition of the founding period in America, and it made him the recognised master of the method: he travelled and corresponded to copy and to purchase manuscripts, drew the historical societies into systematic work, and was the first American to hold a professorship of history, which he filled at Harvard. His life of the governor Morris of the Constitutional Convention, his collection of the writings of Washington with a history of his presidency, and his Library of American Biography, with its many volumes of the short life, made the biography of the republic a proper literary work for a generation of American readers. Public office followed his letters: he was chosen governor of Massachusetts, served in the Senate of the United States, and was placed at the head of Harvard College in 1849, which he governed until his resignation in 1853 left him free to return to his collections of documents and his editing of the records of the Revolution. He died at Cambridge on 14 March 1866, and was buried in the suburban cemetery there, the most employed and most copied American editor of his day, and the man by whom the public records of the founding period were first made accessible to historians.
literary_profile: His works are editorial, biographical and historical rather than imaginative: the twelve volumes of the Diplomatic Correspondence of the Revolution, the writings and the correspondence of the first president with a history of his administration, the memoirs and correspondence of the diplomatist of the Convention, the national biographical library and its many Lives, his reports and addresses on the historical manuscripts in Europe and at home, the editions of the treaties and of the public records, and the discourses, reviews and addresses on American history which he delivered to societies and on public occasions. He wrote, too, histories and biographies for schools and kept a great correspondence on the collecting and the publication of records; his editorial method - the transcription, the collation, the note and the biographical preface - was for forty years the American standard.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, careful, circumstantial and entirely unadorned prose, whether in the editorial preface, the note on a document or the biographical narrative; a habit of arrangement and of chronological and documentary evidence in place of argument or colour; in the Lives a brief, respectable and fact-laden manner which supplies the dates and the papers rather than the character; and in the Addresses and reviews a formal and patriotic diction of the historical societies of the period.
intellectual_concerns: The preservation and right reading of national records as a public duty; the diplomacy, the institutions and the motive of the Revolution as documentary history; the education of a republican people through biography and through exact narrative; the relation of the scholar to the state and to the college; the religious and civic obligations of the Unitarian ministry and of the historical society; the character and the motives of the founders, studied in their own letters.
historical_significance: He created the American documentary edition and with it the modern American historical profession's apparatus: the Diplomatic Correspondence, the Washington and the Morris collections and the national biography set the standard of scholarly editing and of public provision for records, and his advocacy gave the historical societies their work and the state legislature its first appropriations. As the first professor of history in the United States, as the editor whose methods were imitated for half a century, and as the minister, governor, senator and president of Harvard who joined letters to office, he is the type of the man of letters as a national institution in the generation before the Civil War.
major_influences: The self-education of the New England country school and the academy at Exeter
the Unitarian ministry and the Boston circle about the review he conducted
George Washington and the founding records themselves as the objects of his life's work
the British editorial and documentary practice of the record commissions
the historical and biographical writing of the early American societies
the example and the papers of the statesmen whose lives he edited
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of his Harvard course and of his first settled ministry, and the order of his Ohio years, are stated variously in the memoirs and in the biographical dictionaries, the chronology of his share in the conduct of the review being complicated by the anonymous practice of the journal; some of the anecdotes of his poverty and of his western years depend upon the memoir written by himself and by his family.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England letters of Hartford and New Haven in the 1780s, and the revolutionary and deist circle of Americans and French philosophes in the 1790s
literary_identity: Epic poet of the New World, didactic and mock-heroic verse writer, deist controversialist, farmer of America's first great poem on its own subject, and the American diplomat who ended his life on the retreat from Moscow; the most considerable and most compromised American poet of the generation before Bryant.
biography: Barlow was born at Redding in Connecticut, of farming stock with a New England schoolmaster's ambition attached to it, and was put forward to Yale, where he graduated in 1778 of the class which gave the American republic some of its best-known scholars and writers. He served as a chaplain with the Continental forces for three years during the Revolution, was afterwards a tutor at Yale, and belonged in the 1780s to the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of wits who wrote the burlesque and satirical miscellany of the Federalist years, from which he parted company in religion and politics as the French Revolution divided American opinion. He removed to France, where he lived for the rest of his life with short absences, wrote and published the poem on Columbus which he had begun in America, and became an active friend of the American and French reformers; his marriage, his residence near Paris and his correspondence made him the centre of a small American colony in revolutionary France. He was employed by his government in the negotiation of the peace with the regency of Algiers, and was afterwards sent as minister to France; but he had taken French naturalization and had been chosen into the revolutionary legislature, the Directory declined to receive an American minister who was also a citizen of France, and his Federalist countrymen regarded him from that time as something little short of a renegade. He wrote the enlarged and sumptuously given epic of the New World which succeeded the Vision of Columbus, the mock-heroic poem on a New England dish which is still the most agreeable of his verse, and much pamphlet and controversial matter on the politics and the religion of the two countries between which his life was divided; he was also the friend and defender of the age's most infamous radical writer, whose last papers he had the handling of. He accompanied the French army into Russia in 1812 in a department of supply, and, worn out and sick, died at Zarnowiec on the retreat from Moscow on 26 December 1812, leaving a grave in a Polish village churchyard and an almost wholly forgotten epic.
literary_profile: His work is epic, didactic and occasional verse, a body of political and religious pamphlet writing, and a large correspondence: the Columbus poem first printed in 1787, recast and greatly enlarged as the national epic of 1807 with a train of illustrative notes and dissertations on the science, the history and the geography of the New World; the mock-heroic poem on a New England pudding, written abroad and the best-known of his shorter pieces; and prose arguments on deist and Unitarian theology, on education, on the slave trade and on the politics of the French Revolution. The epic was designed as a work of the American continent - its discovery, its colonization, its war and its future - and it is the largest attempt at a national poem made in America before the nineteenth century was well advanced.
stylistic_characteristics: A command of the eighteenth-century heroic couplet, fluent, descriptive and argumentative, and a blanket ambition of scale in the epic which outruns the execution: enumeration, prophecy, apostrophe to the continent, and a didactic paraphrase of science and history in verse. The lower and better manner is the easy narrative and the joke - the mock-heroic exaltation of a country dish - and the prose is plain, urgent and often sarcastic, with the controversialist's habit of the numbered argument.
intellectual_concerns: The moral and providential destiny of America, and the use of the epic to a republic; the progress of knowledge, agriculture and civil society; deist and anti-Trinitarian religion against the creeds of New England Calvinism; the rights of man, representative government and the causes of the French Revolution; the slave trade and the condition of the poor; the education of a national taste and a national language.
historical_significance: He wrote the first ambitious American epic and the first American poem to take the whole continent and its history as its subject, and his attempt, ridiculed by the British review press and abandoned by American readers, defined the problem of the long American poem for the generation of Bryant and of the Knickerbocker writers. His diplomatic business with the Barbary regency belongs to the early foreign history of the republic, his religious and political writings carry American deism and republicanism into the European circle of the 1790s, and his career is the clearest case of the American man of letters divided between the revolution he celebrated and the country that distrusted him.
major_influences: Alexander Pope and the Augustan couplet
John Milton and the epic machinery
James Thomson and the British descriptive school
Thomas Paine and the deist and republican writing of the 1790s
Joseph Priestley and the rational dissenting theology
his Yale tutors and the New England college rhetoric
the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of Federalist wits, from whom he differed
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of his marriages and of his first wife's death, and the chronology of the several recensions and issues of the Columbus poem, are imperfectly recorded; his acceptance of French naturalization and his election to the Council of Five Hundred are stated variously by hostile Federalist accounts and by the later defence of his family, which extenuated them; and the details of the journey of 1812 and of his death rest on the letters of his companions and on local tradition at Zarnowiec.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world and the aggressive New England literary nationalism that preceded the Young America movement
literary_identity: Novelist, poet, critic, editor and lecturer, the most combative and most influential American reviewer of the 1810s and 1820s, the chief American champion of Byron and of the new British and German poetry, and the boldest early claimant of an American literature independent of English judgment.
biography: Neal was born at Portland in the district of Maine, then part of Massachusetts, of a family of small means; his father was a schoolmaster, the household fell into difficulty early, and the boy was put behind a shop counter instead of being sent to a college. Largely self-taught, he was bound to learn law and read it, went to Baltimore in 1816, was admitted to the bar there but practised little, and gave himself to the newspapers and the weekly literary journals of the city. He edited at Baltimore a short-lived review of arts and books called The Portico in 1818, and for a season a political paper; his poems of 1819 and 1820, his frontier tale of 1822 and his novel of the revolutionary year followed fast, and made him the most forward and most quarrelsome of the young American men of letters. His survey of American writing, contributed to a Scottish monthly from the winter of 1824 into 1825, was the first attempt to take the whole of the native literature as a single history and made him the most quoted critic of the decade. He passed to England in 1823 and remained in London and on the continent until 1827, knew the painters, publishers, reformers and periodical writers of the London literary world, contributed at length to the Edinburgh magazine which had taken him up, and in those years made the acquaintance of the young American poet of the Baltimore and Richmond periodicals whose cause he afterwards pleaded against his own former friends. His novels of the later 1820s, which turned to colonial history and to social and religious doctrine, sold poorly and one of them provoked a scandal of its own; he married in 1828, and after a return to Portland he gradually reinvented himself as the respected man of letters of his native city, writing history and biography for young readers, reminiscence and domestic papers, lecturing on American society, and taking part in civic, temperance and charitable work. He died at Portland on 20 June 1876, having long abandoned the aggressive manner that had made his name notorious, and leaving a body of criticism which the twentieth century reprinted as the founding document of American literary nationalism.
literary_profile: His work covers almost every province of the letters of his generation: verse in the Byronic and the descriptive manner, tales and novels of border adventure, society and doctrine, a large body of critical and programmatic prose, editorial miscellany, lectures, reminiscence and autobiography. His critical papers are the first sustained American argument for literary nationalism and for a realism of language and character, and they attacked at once the caution of American letters and its deference to Edinburgh and London. His fiction is experimental in scale and in manner, opening the Revolution and the western settlements to a colloquial, sensational and digressive narrative voice; the later books on the founders of independence, on Catholicism and on social questions belong to the respectable Victorian career that succeeded the earlier warfare.
stylistic_characteristics: A deliberate vehemence and abruptness of style, with short paragraphs, exclamations, coined words, Americanisms and colloquialisms forced upon the page, and an incessant personal challenge to reader and opponent alike; in the fiction an expansive, digressive and sensational manner, with direct address, self-quotation, unfinished plots and a roughness of execution that later critics reclaimed as a native modernism. The criticism is aphoristic and combative, the autobiography garrulous and self-justifying.
intellectual_concerns: The independence of American letters from English judgment and imitation; the originality of the individual genius and the cowardice of the deferential critic; realism of language and the dignity of common speech; the claims of the new poetry and of the romance; national character, the Puritan inheritance and the duties of the American writer to his own public; the condition of women, Roman Catholicism, slavery and temperance in their American forms.
historical_significance: He was the first American critic of sustained force and a principal transmitter of the new British and German poetry to American readers, and his demand for an American literature of the present shaped the generation that followed, from the Young America writers to the romancers of the 1840s and 1850s. His survey of American writing supplied the first history of the whole native field and helped make the phrase American literature current; his advocacy was decisive for the American recognition of Edgar Allan Poe, whom he introduced to the Richmond and Philadelphia journals, and his irregular, open-form novels are now read as part of the native origin of American prose fiction.
major_influences: Lord Byron and the Byronic poem
the British and German romantic writing he reviewed, including the lake poets, the Scott romance and the German tale
the Edinburgh and London review and magazine tradition
the periodical and newspaper culture of Baltimore, Philadelphia and London
the New England Calvinist inheritance of his childhood
the friendship and quarrels of the Knickerbocker wits of New York
biographical_uncertainty: Much of his periodical writing of the Baltimore years appeared over shifting names and is still imperfectly identified; the names sometimes proposed for him in general reference works cannot be confirmed, and only the Byronic and Scottish-magazine pen name recorded in his own bibliography is secure; part of his early career is known chiefly from his own later reminiscences, which are self-serving and variously dated.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Hartford literary establishment, and the religious and domestic verse and prose of the New England periodicals and annuals
literary_identity: Poet, essayist and moralist of Hartford, the most widely read American woman poet of the decades between the literary aftermath of the Revolution and the Civil War, and the first American woman to make a recognized professional livelihood by her pen.
biography: Sigourney was born at Norwich in Connecticut, the only child of Ezekiel Huntley, a gardener and general workman of small means, and of Zerviah Wentworth Huntley, and she was named after her father's first wife. Her formal schooling was slight and she was largely self-taught, reading the moral essayists, the poets and the religious writers accessible in a New England household. She kept a little school for young children with a friend in her native town, and in her middle twenties removed to Hartford at the invitation of the painter Daniel Wadsworth to educate the girls of his family; there she opened and for some years conducted a school for young women until her marriage. About those years she began to send verses and moral sketches to the Hartford newspapers and to journals at Washington, Boston and Philadelphia, sometimes signing only her initials, and her occasional poems on bereavement and on public tragedy circulated widely before she had a book. On 16 June 1819 she married Charles Bartlett Sigourney, a printer, publisher and editor of the same city, whose reason gave way in the middle of the next decade and who survived as an invalid until 1831; the support of the household and of her sons thereafter rested on her writing. Her Moral Pieces in Prose and Verse, followed by the Poems of 1827 issued without her name and put forward as the work of the author of the earlier volume, made her at once the most widely read woman poet in the United States, and both books were reissued in enlarged and collected editions through the next thirty years. Letters to Young Ladies and Letters to a Mother, with books of maxims, of daily meditations and of scriptural and historical reading for families, gave her prose a circulation larger still, while her sketch-books of travel in Connecticut and in France, her verses on the murdered missionary family at the western settlement of the Sandusky affair, on Washington, on Napoleon and on the dead of the Mexican war made her the recorded feeling of the middle-class American household for a generation. She corresponded with men and women of letters on both sides of the Atlantic, contributed continuously to the gift-books and monthlies, was among the American correspondents of a household journal edited by Dickens, was honoured with portraits and with tribute volumes from her women readers, and was elected to historical societies. A stroke in her last years did not stop her writing; she died at Hartford on 10 June 1865 and was buried in the hill cemetery there, at her death the best-known American poetess and within two generations an author the schoolbooks had all but forgotten.
literary_profile: Her work divides between short lyrical, elegiac and reflective poems, largely on grief, death, remembrance and the consolation of faith, and prose of moral and domestic instruction: letters and manuals for young women and mothers, sketch-books of travel at home and in France, essays and tales in the manner of the annuals, and books of maxims and daily meditations. She wrote also the elegies and narrative poems on public tragedy and on missionary enterprise for which the women's societies of the day commissioned her, and she supplied the gift-books, the newspapers and the magazines with a steady stream of occasional verse. Her collected poetry appeared in successive enlarged editions and her prose in cheap religious reprints, and the moral earnestness of the pieces carries a social acuteness and a irony that later readers rediscovered.
stylistic_characteristics: A decorous, hymn-like diction in the regular lyric stanza, with abstract and elevated nouns, apostrophe, and an antithetical balance of sorrow and consolation; a pointed, compressed and frequently epigrammatic prose manner, close to the maxim and the daily meditation, with domestic and social observation of character beneath the gravity of tone. Verse on public events becomes more narrative and more rhetorical, and the later pieces on the Civil War are more explicitly political.
intellectual_concerns: Bereavement, mortality and the faith that survives them; the moral agency and the education of women; the religious and charitable duties of the prosperous, including the missionary cause and the treatment of Native Americans; the temperate conduct of public and domestic life; the place of poetry as an instrument of piety, refinement and national memory.
historical_significance: She was the first American woman poet to command a national readership and a professional income, and for thirty years her name stood for the possibility of a female literary career in the United States. Her elegies and domestic verse set the tone of middle-class American mourning and devotion, her commissioning by missionary and charitable societies created the model of the woman writer as public moral servant, and her success prepared the ground for the women's writing of the 1840s and 1850s. Her reputation fell sharply after the century's turn; modern scholarship in American women's writing and in the culture of sentiment has restored her to the history of the period.
major_influences: The New England psalmody and hymn tradition and the Congregational-inherited religion of her childhood
the eighteenth-century moral essay and the familiar prose of the periodical writers
British lake and reflective poetry of the early nineteenth century
the Hartford literary society and the artists and education reformers about her
the annual literary gift-book and the women's missionary and charitable societies

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England Federalist letters of Hartford and New Haven, and the national project of an American language, an American spelling and an American education
literary_identity: Lexicographer, grammarian, orthoepist, schoolbook maker, political pamphleteer and newspaper editor; the man who gave American English its spelling, its schoolbook and its dictionary, and who argued that a republic must have its own language as well as its own government.
biography: Webster was born at West Hartford in Connecticut, of a family of farmers and deacons with a strong notion of learning in it, and was put forward to Yale, whose courses were interrupted by the war, graduating in 1778. He studied law, was admitted to the bar, and found that the law in a new country would not maintain him; for some years he kept schools and taught in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York while he collected materials for a system of English education suited to the United States. The first part of his Grammatical Institute, the spelling book which Americans carried in their satchels for a century, appeared in 1783, and he travelled through the states to introduce it and to persuade the legislatures and the congress to secure to authors and printers a property in their books. He took part in the great argument over the frame of government with an examination of the leading principles of the Constitution, which was among the earliest and most widely read expositions of the new instrument, and he wrote afterward against slavery, against the political and religious consequences of infidelity, and for the measures by which a republic might preserve its character. In 1793 he established at New York the first daily newspaper of that city, a Federalist journal which he conducted for some years and in which he wrote most of its columns himself; he removed to New Haven about 1798 and gave the rest of his life to language, education and religion. His Compendious Dictionary of 1806 was the first considerable dictionary published in the United States, and the two-volume American Dictionary which followed in 1828, prepared with interruptions over more than two decades, with a tour of Europe for the study of the kindred languages and with an enormous correspondence, gave the country its standard of authority in words, its enlarged vocabulary of the arts and of the new republic, and its practical settlement of spelling. He wrote grammars, readers and treatises on the language, revised and corrected the text of the Bible for household reading, took a constant part in the schools, the public affairs and the religious and moral societies of Connecticut, and was a strenuous and sometimes unattractive controversialist on orthography, copyright, education and the temperance of the age. He died at New Haven on 28 May 1843, in possession of a fame which Americans already understood as their own, and was buried in the cemetery there; the property in his dictionary passed into other hands and became, through revision, the great American lexicographical work of the later century.
literary_profile: His writings are a system rather than a set of separate books: the spelling book, grammar and reader which made his name in the schools; the dictionaries of 1806 and 1828, the second built on a great enlarged vocabulary, with illustrations of use and with a preface arguing that language grows from the people who speak it; the political pamphlets of the ratification and of the 1790s; the newspaper columns, letters and dissertations on the language, on the origin of words, on the effects of slavery and on the education of the young; and the religious tracts and Bible revision of his old age. He was also a traveller and a collector of the statistics of the country, and his journals and records amount to an unmatched acquaintance with the speaking and the schooling of the United States.
stylistic_characteristics: In the schoolbooks an economy and practicality of method - the syllabary, the exponent, the table and the lesson - which sets the tone of American instruction and is spare, direct and often bluntly moral; in the prefaces and dissertations a long, argumentative and accumulative prose, full of etymological matter, of tables of pronunciation and of national argument; in the journals of the 1790s a dense, urgent and combative Federalist style; and in the dictionary definitions a precision of generalizing which is the best of his writing.
intellectual_concerns: The relation of a national language to national independence and national character; the reform and fixing of spelling, pronunciation and usage; the education of a republican people and the morals of the common school; copyright and the property of authors; the principles of the Constitution, the danger of French revolutionary opinion, and the sin of slavery; the divine authority and the right reading of the Bible, and the duty of a Christian lexicography.
historical_significance: He made American English a self-respecting standard, and his spelling book and dictionary together gave the United States the orthography and the reference book which still distinguish it from Britain; no single writer did more to create a national medium of instruction, and his argument that language is a national institution passed into the mainstream of American educational and political thought. His dictionary is the foundation of the great American lexicographical tradition, his advocacy helped secure the first American system of protection for authors and printers, and his editorial and political work belongs to the making of the Federalist party and of the American public sphere of the 1790s.
major_influences: Samuel Johnson and the English dictionary tradition
the grammarians and orthoepists of eighteenth-century England
the New England psalter, primer and spelling tradition of his childhood
William Blackstone and the law as he read it
the political writers of the ratification argument
Joseph Addison and the periodical essay as a model for his own journal
the comparative and classical philology which he pursued in Europe and in his correspondence
biographical_uncertainty: The exact periods and places of his schoolkeeping and of his law study are unsettled, and the chronology of the several parts, issues and pirated editions of the spelling book is complicated and variously told; the dates of his European journeys and the extent to which his later dictionaries drew on the collections of his correspondents cannot be precisely measured.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England Congregational letters of Hartford and New Haven, the Yale presidency and the Federalist clerical interest of the 1790s
literary_identity: Preacher, theologian, poet and educator; the president of Yale who made the college the training ground of the New England clergy and of the Federalist interest, the most influential Congregational divine of his generation in America, and the author of the most considerable American descriptive poem of the 1790s.
biography: Dwight was born at Northampton in Massachusetts, of a family long connected with Yale and with the New England ministry, and on his mother's side grandson of the Northampton preacher of the Great Awakening, whose theology and papers were the inheritance of his whole life; he was taught first at home under his mother's direction, reading the classics and the divines before he was a student in the ordinary sense. He entered Yale at thirteen and graduated at seventeen in the class of 1769, taught for two years at the grammar school at New Haven and returned to the college as a tutor, and was licensed to preach in the years of the Revolution, serving with the armies as a chaplain while he preached by contract in the villages of Connecticut and Massachusetts. He came to the public eye as a poet with the epic of the conquest of Canaan published in 1785, belonged in the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of wits whose satires and miscellany defined the Federalist letters of the 1780s, and about 1791 settled at a farm at Greenfield Hill near New Haven, where in the intervals of teaching and preaching he wrote the topographical, historical and didactic poem which bears the place's name. In 1795 he accepted the presidency of Yale, which he held until his death, governing the college through two decades of political agitation, religious revival and war, filling the classes with students from every part of the country, lecturing and preaching against the deistic and revolutionary principles of the age, and superintending an undergraduate community which he treated at once as a school of religion and as a nursery of the New England establishment. His presidency saw the revival of 1802 and the controversies with the Republicans and with the liberal Christians, and he was the most attacked and most quoted clerical Federalist of the embargo years. He wrote much besides: sermons, theological lectures, a defence of the scriptural scheme against the infidelity of the day, biographical and religious memoirs, and the survey of the northern country compiled from the journals of his tours, which was printed from his papers after his death with an enlarged issue following. He died at New Haven on 11 January 1817, having been president of the college for twenty-two years, and was buried in the Grove Street cemetery there, leaving his college the leading school of Congregational New England and his theological writings the standard course of instruction for a generation of ministers.
literary_profile: His verse divides between the early epic on the Israelite conquest, which drew the American continent into the machinery of scriptural history, and the descriptive-poetical essay of Greenfield Hill, which passes from landscape through the settlement, institutions, commerce, religion and morals of the American township. His prose is chiefly clerical and educational: sermons and charges, the theological lectures printed after his death, controversies on the French Revolution and on infidelity, biographical memoirs, religious tracts for the young, and the Travels in New-England and New-York, part journal, part statistical survey and part moral argument, which is the fullest early American example of the traveller's national survey. He edited and used the papers of his grandfather's house, and his editorial and documentary work belongs to the same piety of records which produced the historical societies of the next generation.
stylistic_characteristics: In verse a competent and stately command of the eighteenth-century couplet and of the Thomson and Goldsmith manner of descriptive didactic poetry, with a weight of enumeration, moral reflection and historical recapitalization laid over the landscape; in prose a clear, energetic and frequently contentious pulpit style, argumentative in the theological and political writing, and detailed, table-laden and morally earnest in the Travels, where observation of farms, schools, canals and denominations is always pressed toward religious and civic instruction.
intellectual_concerns: The fate of religion and of sound learning in a republic, and the danger of deistic and revolutionary principles; the Congregational covenant and the education of the ministry; the moral history of New England and the meaning of its townships, colleges and churches; providential national history read through the Bible and through settlement; the duties of the educated to the commonwealth, and the government of students, churches and a people.
historical_significance: As president of Yale for twenty-two years he made the college the central institution of New England Congregationalism and of the Federalist interest, and the ministers, editors and statesmen of the next generation were formed under his government; his theological lectures and his controversies gave the standing clergy their most influential defence against the infidelity of the 1790s and against the rising liberal theology, and his Greenfield Hill was the most ambitious American poem of its decade. His Travels supplied the first systematic portrait of the northern states, and his career remains the type of the American clerical man of letters exercising public influence through an institution.
major_influences: The divinity of his grandfather's house and the Massachusetts Calvinist inheritance
the Scottish moral philosophy and the college exercises at Yale
the British descriptive school of James Thomson and Oliver Goldsmith
the epic and scriptural paraphrase tradition of the eighteenth century
the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of Federalist wits, his friends and opponents in politics
the tours and statistical surveys of the British agricultural and travelling writers

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Unitarian Boston circle of Federal Street and the review writers about Harvard and the Connecticut Valley, and the liberal preaching of New England in the 1820s and 1830s
literary_identity: Preacher and moralist, the most influential religious writer and the most quoted preacher of New England in his generation, the chief expounder of American Unitarianism, and the centre of the Boston circle from which the liberal religion and the liberal literature of New England together proceeded.
biography: Channing was born at Newport in Rhode Island, of a family connected with the commerce and the revolutionary leadership of the State, and was marked early for the professions by a precocity of reading joined to a diffidence of manner. He went to Harvard, graduated in 1798, and earned his living for some years as a tutor in the families of Virginia, where the leisure of the country house gave him his formative reading in the rational dissenting divinity and where, after a season of religious depression and moral struggle, he ceased to believe the doctrines of the Trinity and of the Calvinist scheme of salvation. He was licensed to preach, and in 1803 was settled over the Federal Street congregation at Boston, a church of merchants, physicians, lawyers and scholars, which he served for the rest of his life and which he kept at the centre of the intellectual and charitable affairs of the city. For years he avoided the doctrinal controversy into which his position carried him, preaching instead the moral and religious themes of duty, culture, self-denial and the likeness of man to God, until the occasion of an ordination at Baltimore in May 1819 drew from him the sermon which gave the liberal party its public confession of faith and its answer to the charge of unbelief. From that time he was the most quoted and most attacked divine in the United States; his sermons, discourses and reviews built up a body of practical theology which made the nature of God, the credibility of revelation, the dignity of the human mind and the duties of the Christian the ordinary subjects of American religious discourse. His writings on the character and the treatment of the slave, called out by the violence of the antislavery controversy of the middle and later 1830s, made him an authority on the abolition question and an outlaw in the Southern states, and he was at once a friend, a patron and at last a problem to the younger writers who went beyond him. He was an adviser of education and reform movements, a constant contributor to the American and the British journals, and a preacher whose discourses on public occasions were taken as moral events; the most famous of them gave its name and its programme to a religious party. Failing health sent him in search of strength out of Boston in his last years; he died at Old Bennington in Vermont on 2 October 1842, and was buried in the cemetery at Cambridge, leaving a congregation, a denomination and a generation of preachers formed on his manner.
literary_profile: His works are almost wholly the sermon, the discourse and the review article: the confession of faith of 1819 and the subsequent defences of the Unitarian position against the charges of the Orthodox review press; practical and theological discourses on the attributes of God, on the likeness of the human soul to God, on self-denial, on the culture of the mind, on the union of religious profession with common life, and on the duties of a Christian people; the letters and treatise on slavery; remarks on education, on the character of the age and on the religion of a republic; and a considerable body of review writing on books of theology, history and biography. He projected greater works of history and of doctrinal argument which he never executed, and the journals, letters and conversations of his later years were printed by his family and friends after his death.
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of deliberate, candid and moral argument: the long qualifying sentence, the repeated appeal to reason and to the sentiments, an evident diffidence carrying itself into authority, and a preaching manner that expounds rather than terrifies; the sermon constructed as an essay, with numbered propositions, illustrations from common life and an unction of benevolence; and the review article written with the same courtesy and the same weight of moral assertion.
intellectual_concerns: The unitary being and the moral attributes of God, and the wrong done to them by a creed which divides or debases them; the dignity and capacity of the human soul and its likeness to God as the ground both of religion and of education; the credibility of revelation judged by reason and by the conscience; the duties of self-culture and of the Christian in society; slavery as a national sin and as a trial of character; the union of churches and of the States, and the obligations of the citizen in a republic.
historical_significance: His sermon of 1819 is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a distinct religious body, and through him Boston became the capital of a liberal Protestantism which supplied the clergy, editors and professors of New England for two generations. His writings on the mind, on culture and on the divine humanity prepared the language which the Transcendentalists inherited and reacted against; his public letters on slavery gave the moderate conscience of the North a text; and his preaching remains the standard example of the moral and reasonable sermon in American religious history.
major_influences: Joseph Priestley and the rational dissenting theology which converted him in Virginia
the moral philosophy taught at Harvard out of Joseph Butler and William Paley
the polite English pulpit of John Tillotson and the seventeenth-century devotional writers
the Congregational preaching of the Newport church of his childhood
the British review criticism and the periodical essay
the conversation and philanthropy of the Boston families of his congregation
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of his Virginia tutoring and of the changes of his father's fortunes are given variously, and the exact course of his religious conversion is known chiefly from his own memoranda and from the recastings of his biographers; the chronology of his unpublished projections, and the extent of his share in the journals for which he wrote, are imperfectly reported, and opinions attributed to him on abolition in his last months rest on letters and conversations of doubtful authority.
